newsitem.title: PERU: No end in sight for Peru's hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: No end in sight for Peru's hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels and the Peruvian government showed little sign of resolving their four-day standoff on Saturday, as conditions deteriorated for some 340 hostages still held at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

Although the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels released 38 captives late on Friday, they remained firm in their demand for the release of all jailed comrades and accused the government of "repression" for cutting telephone, water and electricity services at the building.

A statement from the rebels said a "significant" amount of extra hostages would be freed in exchange for being granted telephone contact with the prisoners, but that these releases would not include people "linked to government policy."
Newspapers reported on Saturday that President Alberto Fujimori plans to stay firm in his government's policy of not negotiating with the guerrillas.

"He made it clear that it is not within his plans to negotiate with the subversive group," said the daily Gestion, one of various local newspapers whose editors were invited on Friday by Fujimori to a meeting at Government Palace.
The meeting with the newspaper editors was the only known contact he has had with the media since the crisis began.
Fujimori's government has already rejected freeing MRTA prisoners, and gave no immediate response to the proposal for a phone link with prisons.

The government has positioned more than 900 police and special forces around the ambassador's residence, and has so far rejected pleas from both the rebels and the hostages to restore services to the building.

The hostages include high-ranking government and security officials, among them three ministers and Peru's anti-terrorism police; scores of diplomats including eight ambassadors; and about 40 Japanese businessmen.

As the captives endured a fourth night on the floor in crumpled suits and cramped conditions, the newly freed men told the world of their grueling ordeal and implored authorities to relax their tough stance.

"Cutting off the services does not affect the MRTA, they are used to it," said released hostage Alex Kouri, mayor of Lima's neighbouring port Callao. "The only people who are affected are the hostages."
Civil Defence official Carlos Garcia, added, "They don't have good food. Apart from a meal of chicken and vegetables yesterday, there is only water, bread and cheese inside."
Meanwhile, a Japanese foreign ministry official said on Saturday Japan will send an eight-member medical team to Lima as back-up for local doctors caring for the hostages.
"We have asked the Health and Welfare Ministry to send a group consisting of three doctors, four nurses and one administration official in a day or two to Lima," the official told reporters in Tokyo.

The freed hostages said that at least 22 MRTA guerrillas, using only numbers to identify themselves, kept strict control over the hostages, splitting them into two groups on separate floors with no communication between them.
But they said the men were keeping their spirits up, watching television coverage of the crisis, and playing chess, checkers (draughts) and dominoes.

Red Cross workers collected letters from the hostages for their relatives and also brought in socks, underwear and shirts from family members. They said some captives were suffering from diarrhoea, diabetes, ulcers and heart problems.

The rebels, who came to Lima from the Amazon jungle for the siege, had on Wednesday threatened to start killing their captives if their demands were not met, but have not repeated the threat since then.

Outside the residence, police were becoming restive, but there was no evidence of plans for an assault. "We'd like to go in so that this finishes soon, but we have no orders," said one policeman. "But we're putting on the pressure, right? What we must do is reduce their moral."
Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, in Lima since Thursday, led Tokyo's effort to persuade Fujimori to maintain a cautious, go-slow approach in negotiations with the MRTA.
Fujimori assured (U.S.) President Bill Clinton he would do so, but the plans of the enigmatic Peruvian leader, better known for strong-arm tactics than diplomacy, were unclear.
Under international law, the ambassador's residence is considered Japanese territory so Fujimori must seek Tokyo's permission before taking any military action.

A man claiming to be an MRTA rebel telephoned Lima's CPN radio station on Friday to warn authorities against a raid on the residence. "We don't want any attack or any assault," the unidentified caller said. "We know we're dead anyway and there's nothing left but for us all to die together."

All parties appeared to be preparing themselves for a long haul. Sixteen portable toilets were delivered to the residence, while rows of telephones were set up in the street outside to serve a growing horde of journalists and relatives.

MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini apparently meticulously planned the original assault, which he led from outside via cellular phone, and was believed to be still directing the siege using a two-way radio.
Video footage sent to Panamericana Television by the rebels showed a masked leader demonstrating a scale model of the residence to heavily armed fellow rebels.
